newsitem.title: USA: Former Olympics suspect describes "88 days of hell".
newsitem.headline: Former Olympics suspect describes "88 days of hell".

text.p: Speaking out for the first time since he was branded a suspect in the Olympics bombing, former security guard Richard Jewell on Monday blamed the FBI and the media for almost destroying his life during "88 days of hell."

Flanked by his mother Barbara, three attorneys and the American flag, Jewell spoke for 10 minutes in a nationally televised news conference held two days after the U.S. Justice Department cleared him of suspicion in a FBI investigation of the July 27 attack.

"Today is a new and different day. Part of my nightmare is over. The difficult task of trying to restore my reputation begins," he said, brushing away tears from time to time as his voice broke under the emotional strain.
"I am a citizen with rights, just like everybody else. I am a human being with feelings, just like everybody else."

"In its rush to show the world how quickly it could get its man, the FBI trampled on my rights as a citizen. In its rush for the headline that the hero was the bomber, the media cared nothing for my feelings as a human being."

Once he finished speaking, attorneys for Jewell said they planned to sue U.S. television network NBC, NBC's news anchor Tom Brokaw and the Atlanta Journal-Constitution for allegedly defaming Jewell's character.
"We have already announced, definitely, that we will be suing the Atlanta Journal-Constitution. We've also announced that we will be suing NBC and Tom Brokaw," said Jewell's lawyer Wayne Grant.
The attorneys also are considering legal action against the federal government and said they will examine any possible role played by the Atlanta Committee for the Olympic Games.

Jewell, 33, was working as a private security guard near Centennial Olympic Park in downtown Atlanta July 27 when he spotted a suspicious green knapsack that had been left unattended at a crowded outdoor concert.

He alerted police and helped clear revelers from the area before a pipe bomb inside the sack detonated at 1:20 a.m., sending nails and other shrapnel tearing through the crowd. Two people died as a result of the blast and more than 100 others were injured.
Jewell initially was hailed as a hero for his actions. But on July 30 an article in the Atlanta Journal-Constitution named him as a focus of the investigation.

Until Saturday, when U.S. Attorney Kent Alexander issued a letter exonerating him of any involvement, Jewell said he spent "every waking minute afraid that I would be arrested and charged with a horrible crime, a crime I did not commit.
"I felt like a hunted animal, followed constantly, waiting to be killed," he said.
But Jewell and his attorneys say the letter has not been enough to clear his name.
Civil lawyer Lin Wood said Jewell was named a suspect on the day Centennial Olympic Park reopened after the bombing and said authorities needed to show the public that the facility was safe.
G. Watson Bryant, Jewell's chief attorney, said the FBI pretended to question his client about the bombing for a training film while trying to get him to waive his rights.
The FBI later denied to Bryant that Jewell was a target, as the attorney clutched a copy of the Atlanta Journal with the front-page headline: "FBI Suspects Hero Guard May Have Planted Bomb."
Separately the U.S. Attorney's Office released partially blanked-out search warrant affidavits that indicated why Jewell was at first singled out as a suspect.
Jewell's attorneys blasted the documents, which contained more than a dozen interviews with acquaintances, as being "painfully thin" and full of "half truths."
"Every American ought to be scared to death about how little it takes for the government to search your property," said Bryant.
